deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It holds Riemann's reading notes and excerpts on Theodor Waitz's article 'Die realistische und naturwissenschaftliche Psychologie', which appeared in the Allgemeine Monatsschrift für Wissenschaft und Literatur (J. G. Droysen was among its editors), August 1853, pp. 655ff. 'Riemann 18' at the top is an archival shelf mark. The notes follow Waitz's sorting of contemporary psychology into two camps.

(1) Realistic (Herbartian) psychology.
- Quoted praise: 'Herbart war der Erste, der mit der Aufsuchung psychologischer Gesetze Ernst gemacht hat.'
- Then a critical remark, probably Riemann's own: Waitz (W.) misreads Herbart's grounding of psychology in metaphysics. He takes it to mean that the premises of psychology must be proved metaphysically. In fact metaphysics only supplies the norms for what can count as an ultimate explanatory ground and what cannot. That is, it decides whether a system of hypotheses can be an ultimate ground or must itself be explained further.
- Next come Schilling and Volkmann: W. F. Volkmann, 'Die Lehre von den Elementen der Psychologie als Wissenschaft' (Prag 1850); G. Schilling, 'Lehrbuch der Psychologie' (Leipzig 1851). They prove metaphysically the unchangeability and qualitative simplicity of the 'Reale' (to be thought of as a being). This is set against Waitz, 'Lehrbuch der Psychologie' S. 16. The arguments listed rest on:
  - the form of unity belonging to all products of inner life;
  - the content of experience as such (reality, intensity), represented as a play of relations and differences.
  The wording of this part is barely legible.
- Drobisch and Hartenstein are presented as forerunners of mathematical psychology. Cited: Drobisch, 'Empirische Psychologie nach naturwissenschaftlicher Methode' (Leipzig 1842) and 'Erste Grundlehren der mathematischen Psychologie' (Leipzig 1850).

(2) Natural-scientific psychology (materialism?).
- Heading: 'Seelenvermögen' (faculties of the soul).
- Beneke starts from the four general basic processes of psychic development. The first two appear on this page: the formation of sensations/perceptions through external stimuli, and the continual regeneration of the primitive faculties ('Urvermögen'). The next page continues with the other two: the striving for equalization of the mobile elements, and the attraction of the like. It then gives Beneke's inference that the soul is immaterial.

Right column: an excerpt from Waitz p. 658 (lower part) defining natural-scientific method. Such inquiry:
- adheres, without metaphysical presuppositions, to the empirical study of a given domain of phenomena;
- tries to obtain from it the explanatory grounds of their connection;
- follows initially hypothetical grounds by strict logic into their consequences;
- tests those consequences against the facts;
- sees the goal of science in knowledge of the laws of events and their necessary connection.

There is no derivation to reconstruct. The page documents Riemann's study of Herbartian and post-Herbartian psychology around 1853. This fits his self-description as a Herbartian in psychology and epistemology, and his published philosophical fragments.

results.what: Reading notes on Waitz's 1853 survey of Herbartian vs. natural-scientific psychology, with Riemann's defence of Herbart: metaphysics gives norms for admissible ultimate explanatory grounds rather than proving psychological premises
results.modern_name: Philosophy of psychology / methodology of science (Herbartian epistemology)
results.usually_credited_to: Herbart; discussed by Waitz, Drobisch, Volkmann, Beneke

deep.surprise_reason: These are bibliographic and philosophical reading notes with no mathematical content. Riemann's Herbartian interests and philosophical fragments are well known; this page adds only minor documentary detail about what he read around 1853.
transcription_corrections: Line 1–2: the cancelled word is probably an abortive 'Augsb.'. The journal is the 'Allgemeine Monatsschrift für Wissenschaft und Literatur' (Droysen among the editors), August 1853, p. 655 — this reading looks right.

Beneke's first basic process probably reads something like 'das sinnliche Wahrnehmen (or: die Bildung der Wahrnehmungen) in Folge von äusseren Reizen', not 'das Bilden neuer Urvermögen'. The second, 'die fortwährende Regeneration', continues onto the next page as '[der] Urvermögen'.
'Drobisch und Hartenstein. Naturwissenschaftliche [?]' — the word after the names is uncertain in the image. It may be a different term, perhaps 'Statik/Mechanik'-related. Keep it flagged.
Insertion 'vier' above 'allgemeinen Grundprozessen' is correct: Beneke's four Grundprozesse, two of which continue on the next page.
'(cf. Waitz Lehrbuch der Psychologie S. 16)' refers to Waitz, Lehrbuch der Psychologie als Naturwissenschaft (1849).
